subtitle: Verified Answer Key (100/100 Qs) + Crisp Simple-English Explanations

items.title: Q1 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation · Unit II: Poetry · John Skelton
items.stem: Who among the following is an early Tudor poet?
items.explanation: John Skelton (c. 1463–1529), Poet Laureate and tutor to the future King Henry VIII known for his rapid 'Skeltonic' verse, was an early Tudor poet, whereas Geoffrey Chaucer, William Langland, and John Gower were fourteenth-century Middle English (Ricardian) poets.

items.title: Q2 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit I: Drama · John Milton
items.stem: Which of the following works of Milton seeks to adapt the form of Greek tragedy?
items.explanation: Published in 1671 alongside Paradise Regained, John Milton's Samson Agonistes is a closet drama explicitly modeled on the form and structure of ancient Greek tragedy, featuring a Chorus, messenger speeches, and strict adherence to the classical unities.

items.title: Q3 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Ted Hughes
items.stem: Ted Hughes' Wodwo is
options: a volume named from the wild men of the woods of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.
a volume named after the elves of the masque of The Tempest.
a volume named after the central character of Pearl.
a volume named after the name of the monster of Beowulf.
items.explanation: Ted Hughes's 1967 collection Wodwo (combining poems, short stories, and a radio play) takes its title and epigraph from the 'wodwos'—the wild men or forest spirits mentioned in line 721 of the fourteenth-century Middle English romance Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.

items.title: Q4 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Allen Ginsberg, Jack Kerouac, Rita Dove
items.stem: Who among the following was NOT a member of the Beat Generation?
items.explanation: African American poet Rita Dove (born 1952), who served as U.S. Poet Laureate from 1993 to 1995 and won the Pulitzer Prize for Thomas and Beulah (1986), was not a member of the 1950s Beat Generation, whose core writers included Allen Ginsberg, Jack Kerouac, and Gregory Corso.

items.title: Q5 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Imtiaz Dharker
items.stem: Purdah is a collection of poems by
items.explanation: Purdah and Other Poems (1989) is the acclaimed debut poetry collection of Pakistan-born British poet and artist Imtiaz Dharker, exploring themes of the veil, gender, identity, and cultural displacement.

items.title: Q6 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Oodgeroo Noonuccal (Kath Walker)
items.stem: Who among the following is an Australian Aboriginal poet?
items.explanation: Kath Walker (later known by her traditional name Oodgeroo Noonuccal, 1920–1993) was a pioneering Australian Aboriginal poet and civil rights activist whose collection We Are Going (1964) was the first book of poetry published by an Aboriginal Australian.

items.title: Q7 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Who among the following built the Red Lion in Stepney in 1567?
items.explanation: In 1567, London grocer John Brayne (brother-in-law of James Burbage) financed and built the Red Lion at Mile End in Stepney, the earliest known purpose-built Elizabethan playhouse in London.

items.title: Q8 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Mention the year in which Political Shakespeare edited by Jonathan Dollimore and Alan Sinfield was published.
items.explanation: Political Shakespeare: New Essays in Cultural Materialism, jointly edited by Jonathan Dollimore and Alan Sinfield and regarded as the foundational text of British Cultural Materialism, was first published in 1985.

items.title: Q9 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Name the play during the performance of which the Globe Theatre was burned down in 1613.
items.explanation: On 29 June 1613, the first Globe Theatre burned to the ground when wadding from a theatrical cannon ignited the thatched roof during a performance of William Shakespeare and John Fletcher's history play Henry VIII (then titled All Is True).

items.title: Q10 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Tony Kushner
items.stem: Who among the following has written the play Angels in America?
items.explanation: Angels in America: A Gay Fantasia on National Themes (1991–92) is a Pulitzer Prize-winning two-part play written by American playwright Tony Kushner, examining the AIDS crisis and Reagan-era politics in 1980s New York.

items.title: Q11 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Name the book in which Peter Brook makes a study of late 1940s theatre.
options: Around the Absurd: Essays on Modern and Postmodern Drama
items.explanation: In his landmark theatre study The Empty Space (1968), British director Peter Brook reflects on post-WWII and late 1940s theatre and divides dramatic performance into four categories: Deadly, Holy, Rough, and Immediate Theatre.

items.title: Q12 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Jane Austen
items.stem: In which novel of Jane Austen is Captain Frederick Wentworth a character?
items.explanation: Captain Frederick Wentworth is the central male protagonist of Jane Austen's final completed novel, Persuasion (published posthumously in 1817), who returns as a wealthy naval officer eight years after Anne Elliot was persuaded to break off their engagement.

items.title: Q13 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charlotte Bronte, Matthew Arnold
items.stem: Who, among the following, wrote about Charlotte Brontë that her mind contained 'nothing but hunger, rebellion, and rage'?
items.explanation: In an April 1853 letter commenting on Charlotte Brontë's recently published novel Villette, Victorian poet and critic Matthew Arnold famously remarked that Brontë's mind contained 'nothing but hunger, rebellion, and rage.'

items.title: Q14 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem:
From which novel of Charles Dickens are the following lines extracted?
"I took her hand in mine, and we went out of the ruined place; and, as the morning mists had risen long ago when I first left the forge, so, the evening mists were rising now, and in all the broad expanse of tranquil light they showed to me, I saw no shadow of another parting from her."
items.explanation: These are the famous closing lines of the published (revised) ending of Charles Dickens's Great Expectations (1861), in which Pip and Estella walk hand in hand out of the ruined garden of Satis House.

items.title: Q15 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · George Eliot
items.stem: Adam in Adam Bede of George Eliot is a
items.explanation: In George Eliot's first novel Adam Bede (1859), the title character Adam Bede is a tall, skilled, and upright village carpenter living in the rural community of Hayslope.

items.title: Q16 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Edgar Allan Poe
items.stem: Who among the following has written Tales of the Grotesque and Arabesque?
items.explanation: Tales of the Grotesque and Arabesque (published in two volumes in late 1839, dated 1840) is a landmark collection of Gothic and psychological short stories—including 'The Fall of the House of Usher'—written by American author Edgar Allan Poe.

items.title: Q17 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Raja Rao
items.stem: The name of the Goddess in Kanthapura is:
items.explanation: In Raja Rao's novel Kanthapura (1938), Kenchamma ('Kenchamma, Great Goddess, Benign One') is the local presiding gramadevata (village goddess) of Kanthapura who protects the villagers from famine, disease, and misfortune.

items.title: Q18 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Margaret Atwood, Margaret Laurence
items.stem: Which of the following is NOT written by Margaret Atwood?
items.explanation: The Stone Angel (1964), the first novel in the Manawaka series featuring the ninety-year-old narrator Hagar Shipley, was written by Canadian novelist Margaret Laurence, not Margaret Atwood. The Edible Woman (1969), Surfacing (1972), and The Handmaid's Tale (1985) are all novels by Margaret Atwood.

items.title: Q19 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: The author of The Golden Bough, a text that influenced Eliot's poetry and criticism substantially, is
items.explanation: Scottish social anthropologist Sir James George Frazer authored The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (first edition 1890), whose accounts of vegetation myths and the Fisher King deeply influenced T.S. Eliot's The Waste Land (1922).

items.title: Q20 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · William Empson
items.stem: Seven Types of Ambiguity was published in the year
items.explanation: William Empson's foundational work of close reading, Seven Types of Ambiguity—written while he was studying under I.A. Richards at Cambridge—was first published in 1930.

items.title: Q21 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas Carlyle
items.stem: The debate on 'the condition of England question' was initiated by
items.explanation: Victorian sage writer Thomas Carlyle coined the phrase and initiated the debate on the 'Condition-of-England Question' in the opening chapter of his 1839 pamphlet Chartism, addressing the social misery of the industrial working class.

items.title: Q22 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · John Dryden
items.stem: The character who discusses the relative merits of French drama and English drama in Essay of Dramatic Poesy is:
items.explanation: In John Dryden's Of Dramatick Poesie, An Essay (1668), the debate comparing the relative merits of French and English drama is conducted between Lisideius (representing Sir Charles Sedley, who praises French neoclassical drama) and Neander (Dryden, who defends English drama and tragicomedy).

items.title: Q23 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Saussure delivered his series of lectures on general linguistics, later published after his death as Course in General Linguistics, at the University of
items.explanation: Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure delivered his three landmark lecture courses on general linguistics between 1907 and 1911 at the University of Geneva; after his death, his colleagues Charles Bally and Albert Sechehaye compiled them into Course in General Linguistics (1916).

items.title: Q24 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Noam Chomsky is known for his
items.explanation: American linguist Noam Chomsky is renowned for formulating the theory of Generative Grammar (and Transformational-Generative Grammar), first introduced in Syntactic Structures (1957), which models the innate rule system underlying human language.

items.title: Q25 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Jacques Lacan
items.stem: The 'Name of the Father' is a term made famous by
items.explanation: French psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan coined the concept of the 'Name-of-the-Father' (le Nom-du-Père) in his 1950s seminars to denote the paternal legislative function and prohibition that initiates the child into the Symbolic order of language and law.

items.title: Q26 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Edward Said, Roland Barthes
items.stem: Which among the following books is NOT written by Edward Said?
options: On Late Style: Music and Literature against the Grain
The World, the Text and the Critic
items.explanation: Image-Music-Text (1977) is a famous collection of essays by the French literary theorist and semiotician Roland Barthes, whereas On Late Style (2006), The World, the Text, and the Critic (1983), and The Question of Palestine (1979) were written by Edward W. Said.

items.title: Q27 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: What does Pierre Bourdieu imply by the term 'habitus' in his sociological studies?
options: The culture of increasing consumerisation of post-capitalist societies.
The phenomenon of the masses succumbing to material fetishism of different types.
A person's posture, speech and the mental habit of perception, classification, appreciation, feeling and action.
Personal habits that do not impact the society profoundly.
items.explanation: In Pierre Bourdieu's sociology (such as Outline of a Theory of Practice and Distinction), 'habitus' refers to the socially ingrained system of durable dispositions—including bodily posture, speech, and mental habits of perception, classification, appreciation, feeling, and action.

items.title: Q28 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem: Donna Haraway's "Cyborg Manifesto" underscores the notion that -
options: the boundaries between animal, human and machine are breaking down.
the cyborgs would establish a dictatorship of the proletariat in the near future.
humans and non-humans would wage a battle for acquisition of cultural capital.
identity politics would be bolstered by intervention of artificial intelligence.
items.explanation: In her landmark essay 'A Cyborg Manifesto' (1985), feminist scholar Donna Haraway argues that in late twentieth-century technoculture, three crucial boundaries have broken down: those between human and animal, between organism (animal-human) and machine, and between the physical and non-physical.

items.title: Q29 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem: The concept of the public sphere plays a particularly important role in the work of
items.explanation: German Frankfurt School philosopher and sociologist Jürgen Habermas formulated the influential concept of the 'public sphere' (Öffentlichkeit) in his book The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962).

items.title: Q30 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Samuel Johnson
items.stem: An Account of the Life of Mr Richard Savage, Son of the Earl Rivers (1744) was the first major biography published by
items.explanation: An Account of the Life of Mr Richard Savage, Son of the Earl Rivers (1744) was the first major literary biography written by Samuel Johnson, chronicling the turbulent life of his friend and fellow poet Richard Savage and later incorporated into Johnson's Lives of the Poets.

items.title: Q31 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Thomas Love Peacock
items.stem: Thomas Love Peacock authored the essay
options: "An Essay on the Principles of Human Action"
items.explanation: Thomas Love Peacock authored the satirical essay 'The Four Ages of Poetry' (1820), dividing poetry into Iron, Gold, Silver, and Brass ages and famously provoking Percy Bysshe Shelley to write A Defence of Poetry (1821).

items.title: Q32 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · John Locke
items.stem: Who proposed the idea that the mind at the time of birth is like a blank slate or tabula rasa?
items.explanation: In An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689/1690), English empiricist philosopher John Locke rejected innate ideas and argued that the human mind at birth is a 'white paper, void of all characters' (tabula rasa or blank slate) furnished entirely through sensory experience and reflection.

items.title: Q33 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Umberto Eco
items.stem: The Aesthetics of Thomas Aquinas is written by
items.explanation: The Aesthetics of Thomas Aquinas (originally published in Italian in 1956 as Il problema estetico in San Tommaso) was the doctoral dissertation and first published book of Italian semiotician, medievalist, and novelist Umberto Eco.

items.title: Q34 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Francis Bacon
items.stem: Francis Bacon's The Advancement of Learning was dedicated to
items.explanation: Published in 1605, Sir Francis Bacon's philosophical treatise Of the Proficience and Advancement of Learning, Divine and Human was dedicated to King James I of England, praising the monarch's erudition and appealing for royal patronage of scientific inquiry.

items.title: Q35 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas Hobbes
items.stem: Thomas Hobbes's philosophical tract Leviathan was first published in
items.explanation: Thomas Hobbes's landmark work of social-contract political philosophy, Leviathan, or The Matter, Forme and Power of a Common-Wealth Ecclesiasticall and Civil, was first published in 1651 during the English Interregnum.

items.title: Q36 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Who among the following argued that children learn language based on behaviorist reinforcement principles by associating words with meaning?
items.explanation: In Verbal Behavior (1957), American psychologist B.F. Skinner argued from a behaviorist perspective that children learn language through operant conditioning, imitation, and reinforcement principles by associating words with meanings.

items.title: Q37 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: The full form of MLAT is
items.explanation: In applied linguistics and language testing, MLAT stands for the Modern Language Aptitude Test, a standardized assessment developed by John B. Carroll and Stanley Sapon in 1959 to measure foreign language learning aptitude.

items.title: Q38 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem: The Kothari Commission suggested
options: that English must be used as a link language to translate one Indian language text into another.
that English be studied as a library language with the aim of getting the knowledge of science and technology, commerce and trade by reading standard books in English.
that research in India should be done only in English.
that a teacher at a University must know how to speak and write in English.
items.explanation: The Indian Education Commission (1964–1966), chaired by Dr. D.S. Kothari, famously recommended that English should serve as a vital 'library language' in higher education so students could access world knowledge in science, technology, and commerce.

items.title: Q39 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: A structured interview consists of
options: a series of pre-determined questions along with questions asked at the time of the interview.
a series of questions on the structure of the research.
items.explanation: In research methodology, a structured interview is a quantitative or standardized interview format consisting of a fixed series of pre-determined questions administered in the exact same wording and sequence to all respondents.

items.title: Q40 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: Which of the following methods is used to study the diversity of human cultures in their particular cultural settings?
items.explanation: Ethnography is the qualitative research method rooted in cultural anthropology that uses immersive fieldwork and participant observation to study the diversity of human cultures and communities within their natural cultural settings.

items.title: Q41 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) · Unit II: Poetry · John Dryden
items.stem:
Which among the following is true about Religio Laici?
A. John Dryden wrote Religio Laici.
B. Religio Laici strongly criticized the Anglican Church.
C. Religio Laici means 'A Layman's Faith'.
D. Religio Laici was published in 1690.
E. Religio Laici was a philosophico-religious prose treatise.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: John Dryden wrote Religio Laici (A), which translates to 'A Layman's Faith' (C). Published in 1682 (not 1690), it is a philosophical-religious poem in heroic couplets (not a prose treatise) that defends the Anglican Church's via media against Deism, Catholicism, and Puritanism.

items.title: Q42 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Edward Albee
items.stem:
Which two of the following plays have been written by Edward Albee?
A. The Zoo Story
B. The Price
C. A Delicate Balance
D. Fences
E. Operation Sidewinder
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Zoo Story (1958, A) and the Pulitzer Prize-winning A Delicate Balance (1966, C) are plays written by American dramatist Edward Albee. By contrast, The Price (1968) is by Arthur Miller, Fences (1985) is by August Wilson, and Operation Sidewinder (1970) is by Sam Shepard.

items.title: Q43 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit I: Drama · Nissim Ezekiel
items.stem:
Which three of the following plays have been written by Nissim Ezekiel?
A. Savaksa
B. Marriage-Poem
C. Nalini
D. Mister Behram
E. Sleepwalkers
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Marriage-Poem: A Tragi-Comedy (B), Nalini: A Comedy (C), and Sleepwalkers: An Indo-American Farce (E) were written by Nissim Ezekiel and published together in his Three Plays (1969). Mister Behram (1988) and Savaksa (in Princes, 1970) are associated with Gieve Patel.

items.title: Q44 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit I: Drama · Gurcharan Das, Cyrus Mistry
items.stem:
Which two of the following dramatists have won the Sultan Padamsee Award?
A. Mahesh Dattani
B. Gurcharan Das
C. Girish Karnad
D. Cyrus Mistry
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Gurcharan Das (B) won the inaugural Sultan Padamsee Award for Playwriting in 1968 for his historical play Larins Sahib, and Cyrus Mistry (D) won the Sultan Padamsee Award in 1978 for his play Doongaji House.

items.title: Q45 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit I: Drama · Richard Brinsley Sheridan
items.stem:
Identify the works written by Richard Brinsley Sheridan:
A. Richelieu
B. St. Patrick's Day
C. The Duenna
D. The Citizen of the World
E. Irene
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The farce St. Patrick's Day; or, The Scheming Lieutenant (1775, B) and the comic opera The Duenna (1775, C) were written by Richard Brinsley Sheridan. Richelieu (1839) is by Edward Bulwer-Lytton, The Citizen of the World (1762) is by Oliver Goldsmith, and Irene (1749) is by Samuel Johnson.

items.title: Q46 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Mulk Raj Anand
items.stem:
Which of the following fictional works form a trilogy by Mulk Raj Anand?
A. The Village
B. Private Life of an Indian Prince
C. Across the Black Waters
D. The Sword and the Sickle
E. The Road
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Mulk Raj Anand's famous Lalu Singh trilogy consists of The Village (1939, A), Across the Black Waters (1939, C), and The Sword and the Sickle (1942, D), following the Punjabi peasant Lalu through rural oppression, World War I in Europe, and revolutionary politics in India.

items.title: Q47 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · William Faulkner
items.stem:
Which of the following are written by William Faulkner?
A. Sanctuary
B. Color Struck
C. Jesus, The Son of Man
D. Light in August
E. Absalom, Absalom!
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Sanctuary (1931, A), Light in August (1932, D), and Absalom, Absalom! (1936, E) are modernist Southern Gothic novels written by William Faulkner. Color Struck (1925) is a play by Zora Neale Hurston, and Jesus, the Son of Man (1928) is by Kahlil Gibran.

items.title: Q48 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Arnold Bennett, H. G. Wells, E. M. Forster
items.stem:
Who among the following are called Edwardian Novelists?
A. George Eliot
B. Arnold Bennett
C. H. G. Wells
D. Edward Morgan Forster
E. Robert Louis Stevenson
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Arnold Bennett (B), H.G. Wells (C), and E.M. Forster (D) are major novelists of the Edwardian era (1901–1910/1914), whereas George Eliot (1819–1880) and Robert Louis Stevenson (1850–1894) were Victorian novelists.

items.title: Q49 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Lewis Grassic Gibbon
items.stem:
Lewis Grassic Gibbon's A Scots Quair comprises the following books:
A. Sunset Song
B. Brothers and Sisters
C. Cloud Howe
D. Men and Wives
E. Grey Granite
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Scottish writer Lewis Grassic Gibbon's celebrated trilogy A Scots Quair (collected in 1946), centering on the life of Chris Guthrie, comprises Sunset Song (1932, A), Cloud Howe (1933, C), and Grey Granite (1934, E). Brothers and Sisters (1929) and Men and Wives (1931) are novels by Ivy Compton-Burnett.

items.title: Q50 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Donald Davie, Philip Larkin
items.stem:
The Movement poets included:
A. Donald Davie
B. Hilda Doolittle
C. Michael Longley
D. Philip Larkin
E. Derek Walcott
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Donald Davie (A) and Philip Larkin (D) were prominent members of 'The Movement,' a group of 1950s British poets featured in Robert Conquest's anthology New Lines (1956) who favored anti-romantic wit, formal regularity, and empirical clarity.

items.title: Q51 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · James Fenton, Seamus Heaney, Paul Muldoon
items.stem:
Some of the following poets adorned the Oxford Professor of Poetry Chair:
A. James Fenton
B. Margaret Atwood
C. Seamus Heaney
D. Anne Sexton
E. Paul Muldoon
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Seamus Heaney (1989–1994, C), James Fenton (1994–1999, A), and Paul Muldoon (1999–2004, E) all held the prestigious post of Oxford Professor of Poetry, whereas Canadian writer Margaret Atwood and American confessional poet Anne Sexton never held the chair.

items.title: Q52 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · John Dennis
items.stem:
Which of the following works are written by John Dennis?
A. The Advancement and Reformation of Modern Poetry
B. The Christian Hero
C. The Grounds of Criticism in Poetry
D. The Conscious Lovers
E. An Essay on the Genius and Writings of Shakespeare
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Augustan critic John Dennis wrote The Advancement and Reformation of Modern Poetry (1701, A), The Grounds of Criticism in Poetry (1704, C), and An Essay on the Genius and Writings of Shakespear (1712, E). The Christian Hero (1701) and The Conscious Lovers (1722) were written by Sir Richard Steele.

items.title: Q53 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas Carlyle
items.stem:
Which of the following works have been authored by Thomas Carlyle?
A. Chartism
B. Past and Present
C. The French Revolution
D. Suspiria de Profundis

items.explanation: Victorian historian and social critic Thomas Carlyle authored Chartism (1839, A), Past and Present (1843, B), and The French Revolution: A History (1837, C). Suspiria de Profundis (1845) and The English Mail-Coach (1849) were written by Thomas De Quincey.

items.title: Q54 · June 2023 (Shift 1)

items.stem:
Which among the following is true about corpus linguistics?
A. It is a collection of naturally occurring spoken and written texts.
B. It has ensured the supremacy of speech over writing.

D. It is a methodology that involves computer based empirical analysis of language use.
E. It is a branch of linguistics that is purely based on Chomskyan linguistics.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Corpus linguistics is based on large, principled collections of naturally occurring spoken and written texts (A) and uses computer-assisted empirical methodologies to analyze patterns of real-world language use (D), standing in contrast to purely introspective Chomskyan linguistics.

items.title: Q55 · June 2023 (Shift 1)

B. F. R. Leavis
C. George Saintsbury
D. I. A. Richards
E. William Empson
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: F.R. Leavis (B), I.A. Richards (D), and William Empson (E) are known as the twentieth-century Cambridge Critics who revolutionized English studies at Cambridge University through close reading, practical criticism, and rigorous moral evaluation.

items.title: Q56 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Allen Tate, Cleanth Brooks

E. Paradox
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Tension (coined by Allen Tate, A), Irony (C), and Paradox (championed by Cleanth Brooks in The Well Wrought Urn, E) are core analytical terms of American New Criticism. 'Mirror Stage' belongs to Jacques Lacan's psychoanalysis and 'Polyphony' to Mikhail Bakhtin's dialogism.

E. Modern Painters
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Walter Pater's Studies in the History of the Renaissance (1873, A), Matthew Arnold's 'The Function of Criticism at the Present Time' (1864, D), and John Ruskin's Modern Painters (1843–60, E) are major works of Victorian criticism, whereas Jessie L. Weston's From Ritual to Romance (1920, B) and T.S. Eliot's 'Hamlet and His Problems' (1919, C) belong to the twentieth century.

items.title: Q58 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Theodor Adorno, Max Horkheimer
items.stem:
Facts about the Frankfurt School include the following:

B. Adorno and Horkheimer were its two members.
C. The School established the term 'Critical Theory'.
D. It had strong ties with the thinkers of the Moscow Linguistic Circle.
E. It was forced into exile with the ascendency of Nazism in Germany.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Frankfurt School (Institute for Social Research) was founded in 1923 (not 1925); Theodor Adorno and Max Horkheimer were two of its leading members (B), Horkheimer's 1937 essay established the term 'Critical Theory' (C), and the Institute was forced into exile in 1933 with the rise of Nazism in Germany (E).

items.explanation: Cultural theorist Stuart Hall wrote the landmark media-studies essays 'Encoding/Decoding' (1973/1980, A) and 'The Rediscovery of "Ideology": Return of the Repressed in Media Studies' (1982, B). items.explanation: Hyperreality (A) and Simulacra (D) are the signature concepts of French postmodern theorist Jean Baudrillard, most famously elaborated in Simulacra and Simulation (1981). Bricolage is associated with Lévi-Strauss and Derrida, Rhizome with Deleuze and Guattari, and Dispositif with Foucault.

items.title: Q96 · June 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · I. A. Richards, John Crowe Ransom, Cleanth Brooks
items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow:
At school the study of literature can still involve a close reading or 'practical criticism' of a novel, play or poem without much or any recourse to external material. Practical criticism is the method of analysing a poem, in isolation from the circumstances of its production, developed by I. A. Richards (1893–1979) in the 1920s. He felt that concentration upon 'the words on the page', the technical aspects of the ways verse creates effects, would result in meaningful judgements upon whether a poem was intrinsically 'good' or simply reputedly so. The methodology of practical criticism seeks coherence in images, themes and patterns of language. Richards and his colleagues felt that this practice was 'scientific' and led to objective value judgements. He was part of a group of lecturers at Cambridge University who played a crucial role in the development of the discipline of English Literature and whose methodology influenced the critical practices of the New Critics, John Crowe Ransom (1888–1974) and Cleanth Brooks (1906–94) and their colleagues in the US. Their 'scientific' examination of literature asserted a hierarchy of texts, those that held universal meaning and significance through aesthetic form and those deemed too formulaic to warrant academic scrutiny. The first revered group of texts is often referred to as the literary canon.

In the context of the above passage, close reading implies
options: reading a text by adopting an interdisciplinary mode of inquiry.
reading a text by emphasising on its affective capacity.
reading a text by adopting a phenomenological approach.
reading a text by focussing on words and the technical aspects.
items.explanation: As stated in the passage, close reading or practical criticism involves concentrating directly on 'the words on the page' and the technical aspects of how language, imagery, and verse patterns create meaning in isolation from external biographical or historical context.
